title: Ἄσιος ἐπὶ ταῖς πύλαις
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The poet names the leaders of the five Trojan divisions: Hector, Polydamas and Cebriones; Paris, Alcathous and Agenor; Helenus, Deiphobus and Asius; Aeneas with the two sons of Antenor; and Sarpedon, with Glaucus and Asteropaeus, over the allies. They close ranks behind their oxhide shields and go straight at the ships. All the Trojans and allies have followed Polydamas’ advice and left their chariots at the ditch, except Asius, who will not leave his horses and charioteer, drives up to the ships, and (the poet says) is doomed to die before he gets home, by the spear of Idomeneus. He drives through the gate on the left, which the Achaeans have left open for their own stragglers, and finds two Lapith champions, Polypoetes and Leonteus, standing before it like oaks that wait out wind and rain. Asius’ men come up with their shields held high, and the two Lapiths charge out from the gates and fight like a pair of boars, while from the wall above stones fall as thick as snow. Asius strikes his thighs and cries out against Zeus for deceiving him: the Achaeans, he says, are as unwilling to give ground as wasps and bees. But Zeus wishes glory for Hector and pays him no heed. The poet says that it is hard for him to tell, as a god could, how the fighting went at all the gates, for stone-fire rose all round the wall, the Argives defended their ships out of necessity, and the gods who were their helpers grieved.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἅμ’ Ἕκτορ’ ἴσαν καὶ ἀμύμονι Πουλυδάμαντι,
οἳ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι ἔσαν, μέμασαν δὲ μάλιστα
τεῖχος ῥηξάμενοι κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hoi men ham’ Hektor’ isan kai amymoni Poulydamanti,
hoi pleistoi kai aristoi esan, memasan de malista
teichos rhēxamenoi koilēis epi nēusi machesthai.
sentences.l:
These with Hector went, and with blameless Polydamas,
who were the most numerous and the best, and were most eager
the wall having broken, at the hollow ships to fight.
sentences.i: One division went along with Hector and blameless Polydamas, the largest and the best, and they were keenest of all to break the wall and fight at the hollow ships.
sentences.n: The five divisions were drawn up at the end of the last part; now the poet counts off their leaders. οἳ μέν ‘these, for their part’ is answered by τῶν δ’ ἑτέρων ‘and of the others’ in line 93. ἴσαν is the Homeric imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. Ἕκτορ’ is Ἕκτορι with its ι elided, the dative after ἅμα ‘along with’, and ἀμύμονι Πουλυδάμαντι is also dative. ἀμύμων is a stock epithet, translated ‘blameless’ every time, though its real meaning is not known. οἳ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι ἔσαν is ‘who were the most numerous and the best’ (ἔσαν = ἦσαν). μέμασαν is a perfect-stem form of μάω ‘be eager’, with past sense here, and takes the infinitive μάχεσθαι. ῥηξάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. κοίλῃς is the epic feminine dative plural (Attic κοίλαις) and νηυσί the dative plural of ναῦς.

sentences.t: καί σφιν Κεβριόνης τρίτος εἵπετο·
sentences.tr: kai sphin Kebrionēs tritos heipeto·
sentences.l: and with them Cebriones as third was following;
sentences.i: and Cebriones followed them as the third;
sentences.n: This unit is the first half of line 91. σφιν is the dative plural ‘with them’, Hector and Polydamas, and τρίτος ‘as third’ makes Cebriones the third leader of this division. εἵπετο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. The next unit says why he is free to follow: Hector has put someone else beside the chariot.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἄρ’ ὄχεσφιν
ἄλλον Κεβριόναο χερείονα κάλλιπεν Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.tr:
par d’ ar’ ochesphin
allon Kebrionao chereiona kallipen Hektōr.
sentences.l:
and beside the chariot
another, worse than Cebriones, left behind Hector.
sentences.i: and Hector had left another man beside the chariot, a lesser man than Cebriones.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 91. πὰρ is παρά with its final vowel dropped, and κάλλιπεν is κατέλιπεν, with κατά shortened to κάλ- before the λ. The Greek leaves the man unnamed: ἄλλον is simply ‘another’. χερείονα is the accusative of the comparative χερείων ‘worse’ (Attic χείρων), and Κεβριόναο is the epic genitive in -αο, the genitive of comparison, ‘than Cebriones’. ὄχεσφιν is ὄχεα ‘chariot’ with the ending -φιν, ‘by the chariot’; the plural stands for one vehicle. Line 92 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the syllable να- of Κεβριόναο, which opens the third foot, has to be counted long.

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ ἑτέρων Πάρις ἦρχε καὶ Ἀλκάθοος καὶ Ἀγήνωρ,
sentences.tr: tōn d’ heterōn Paris ērche kai Alkathoos kai Agēnōr,
sentences.l: And of the second Paris was leading, and Alcathous and Agenor;
sentences.i: Paris led the second division, with Alcathous and Agenor;
sentences.n: ἑτέρων is literally ‘other’, but here it opens the count: ‘the second’, followed by τρίτων ‘third’ and τετάρτων ‘fourth’. τῶν is the article as a pronoun, ‘of those’, and ἦρχε takes the genitive, ‘led’. Paris is named first; Alcathous and Agenor are his fellow leaders.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ τρίτων Ἕλενος καὶ Δηΐφοβος θεοειδὴς
υἷε δύω Πριάμοιο·
sentences.tr:
tōn de tritōn Helenos kai Dēïphobos theoeidēs
huie dyō Priamoio·
sentences.l:
And of the third, Helenus and Deiphobus, godlike in form,
the two sons of Priam;
sentences.i: The third was led by Helenus and Deiphobus, godlike in form, the two sons of Priam;
sentences.n: ἦρχε ‘led’ is not repeated from line 93, and τρίτων ‘third’ agrees with an unstated ‘division’. θεοειδής is a stock epithet, translated ‘godlike in form’ every time. υἷε δύω is a dual pair, ‘two sons’, in apposition to Helenus and Deiphobus. The unit ends in the middle of line 95, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τρίτος δ’ ἦν Ἄσιος ἥρως
Ἄσιος Ὑρτακίδης, ὃν Ἀρίσβηθεν φέρον ἵπποι
αἴθωνες μεγάλοι ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος.
sentences.tr:
tritos d’ ēn Asios hērōs
Asios Hyrtakidēs, hon Arisbēthen pheron hippoi
aithōnes megaloi potamou apo Sellēentos.
sentences.l:
and third was Asius the hero,
Asius, Hyrtacus’-son, whom from Arisbe were bearing horses,
fire-bright, big, from the river Selleis.
sentences.i: and the third leader was Asius the hero, Asius, son of Hyrtacus, whom fire-bright and big horses carried from Arisbe, from the river Selleis.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 95. Helenus and Deiphobus are two leaders, so Asius is the τρίτος ‘third’; ἥρως ‘hero’ is the title given to a leader. His name is said twice, the second time with the patronymic Ὑρτακίδης ‘son of Hyrtacus’, which is how he is called through the rest of this part. The last two lines are already in the poem (2.838–839), and the English is the one they have there. ὃν … φέρον is ‘whom … were bearing’, with φέρον an unaugmented imperfect; Ἀρίσβηθεν is ‘from Arisbe’ (-θεν marks the place from which); and ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος has ἄπο after its noun.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ τετάρτων ἦρχεν ἐῢς πάϊς Ἀγχίσαο
Αἰνείας, ἅμα τῷ γε δύω Ἀντήνορος υἷε
Ἀρχέλοχός τ’ Ἀκάμας τε μάχης εὖ εἰδότε πάσης.
sentences.tr:
tōn de tetartōn ērchen eÿs païs Anchisao
Aineias, hama tōi ge dyō Antēnoros huie
Archelochos t’ Akamas te machēs eu eidote pasēs.
sentences.l:
And of the fourth was leading the good son of Anchises,
Aeneas, with him the two sons of Antenor,
Archelochus and Acamas, both knowing all fighting well.
sentences.i: The fourth was led by the good son of Anchises, Aeneas, and with him went the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, who both knew all fighting well.
sentences.n: ἐῢς πάϊς Ἀγχίσαο ‘the good son of Anchises’ stands for Aeneas, who is named in the next line: ἐῢς is ‘good’, πάϊς is παῖς, and Ἀγχίσαο is the epic genitive in -αο. ἅμα τῷ γε is ‘together with him’, τῷ being the article as a pronoun. δύω … υἷε and εἰδότε are duals, ‘the two sons’, ‘both knowing’; εἰδότε takes the genitive μάχης … πάσης, ‘knowing all fighting’, and εὖ goes with it. The last line is already in the poem (2.823), and its English is kept. Line 98 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee (Ἀγ-χί-), and the syllable σα- of Ἀγχίσαο, which opens the sixth foot, has to be counted long.

sentences.t:
Σαρπηδὼν δ’ ἡγήσατ’ ἀγακλειτῶν ἐπικούρων,
πρὸς δ’ ἕλετο Γλαῦκον καὶ ἀρήϊον Ἀστεροπαῖον·
sentences.tr:
Sarpēdōn d’ hēgēsat’ agakleitōn epikourōn,
pros d’ heleto Glaukon kai arēïon Asteropaion·
sentences.l:
And Sarpedon led the renowned allies,
and he took to himself besides Glaucus and warlike Asteropaeus;
sentences.i: Sarpedon led the renowned allies, and took Glaucus and warlike Asteropaeus along with him;
sentences.n: Sarpedon commands the fifth division, the allies. ἡγήσατο is the aorist middle of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’, and takes the genitive ἐπικούρων ‘allies’. ἀγακλειτῶν is ‘renowned’ (ἀγα- strengthens κλειτός ‘famous’). πρὸς … ἕλετο is tmesis for προσαιρέομαι ‘take to oneself in addition’, the preverb πρὸς placed before the δ’. ἀρήϊος is ‘warlike’, the epithet he is given here.

sentences.t:
οἳ γάρ οἱ εἴσαντο διακριδὸν εἶναι ἄριστοι
τῶν ἄλλων μετά γ’ αὐτόν·
sentences.tr:
hoi gar hoi eisanto diakridon einai aristoi
tōn allōn meta g’ auton·
sentences.l:
for they seemed to him outstandingly to be the best
of the others, after himself;
sentences.i: for they seemed to him outstandingly the best of the rest, after himself;
sentences.n: This unit ends in the middle of line 104. οἳ γάρ gives the reason for Sarpedon’s choice. εἴσαντο is the aorist middle of εἴδομαι ‘seem’, here with the infinitive εἶναι and οἱ ‘to him’ (Sarpedon). διακριδόν is ‘outstandingly, pre-eminently’, from διακρίνω ‘pick out’. τῶν ἄλλων μετά γ’ αὐτόν is ‘of the rest, after himself’, the genitive for the group of comparison and μετά with the accusative ‘next after’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔπρεπε καὶ διὰ πάντων.
sentences.tr: ho d’ eprepe kai dia pantōn.
sentences.l: and he stood out even through all.
sentences.i: and he stood out even among them all.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 104. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, Sarpedon, set against the two he has picked. ἔπρεπε is the imperfect of πρέπω ‘stand out, be seen’, and καὶ διὰ πάντων ‘even through all’ means that he shows among every one of them, the best men as well.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἀλλήλους ἄραρον τυκτῇσι βόεσσι
βάν ῥ’ ἰθὺς Δαναῶν λελιημένοι, οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔφαντο
σχήσεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἐν νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν πεσέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei allēlous araron tyktēisi boessi
ban rh’ ithys Danaōn leliēmenoi, oud’ et’ ephanto
schēsesth’, all’ en nēusi melainēisin peseesthai.
sentences.l:
And they, when they had fitted one another with fashioned oxhides,
went straight at the Danaans, eager, and no longer did they say
they would hold back, but upon the black ships would fall.
sentences.i: And when they had locked themselves together with their shields of fashioned oxhide, they went straight at the Danaans, eager, and no longer thought they would hold back, but that they would fall upon the black ships.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, all five divisions together. ἄραρον is the aorist of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, here ‘fitted’ with a double object: ἀλλήλους ‘one another’ and the dative τυκτῇσι βόεσσι ‘with fashioned oxhides’, meaning shields of hide, which they close up edge to edge. τυκτῇσι is the epic dative plural of τυκτός ‘made, fashioned’. βάν ῥ’ is ἔβαν ῥα, the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’; ἰθύς is ‘straight’, here ‘straight at’ with the genitive Δαναῶν; and λελιημένοι is the perfect participle of λελίημαι ‘be eager’. οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔφαντο is ‘and they no longer said’, the subject of the infinitives being the Trojans themselves. The last line is the line that stands in iliad-054 (and is repeated at 126 below), and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι Τρῶες τηλεκλειτοί τ’ ἐπίκουροι
βουλῇ Πουλυδάμαντος ἀμωμήτοιο πίθοντο·
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi Trōes tēlekleitoi t’ epikouroi
boulēi Poulydamantos amōmētoio pithonto·
sentences.l:
Then the other Trojans and the far-famed allies
obeyed the counsel of Polydamas, the faultless;
sentences.i: Then the rest of the Trojans and their far-famed allies did as the faultless Polydamas advised;
sentences.n: ἄλλοι Τρῶες ‘the other Trojans’ are all but Asius, who is set against them in the next unit. βουλῇ πίθοντο is ‘obeyed the counsel’, πίθοντο being the aorist middle of πείθομαι and βουλῇ its dative; the advice is Polydamas’ at 61–79. τηλεκλειτοί is ‘far-famed’ (τηλε- ‘far’, κλειτός ‘famous’), the stock epithet of the allies, and ἐπίκουροι is ‘allies’. ἀμωμήτοιο is the epic genitive of ἀμώμητος ‘without fault’ (from μωμάομαι ‘find fault with’). It is close in sense to ἀμύμων ‘blameless’, whose meaning is not known, and is given a different English, ‘faultless’, so that the two stay apart.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐχ Ὑρτακίδης ἔθελ’ Ἄσιος ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν
αὖθι λιπεῖν ἵππους τε καὶ ἡνίοχον θεράποντα,
ἀλλὰ σὺν αὐτοῖσιν πέλασεν νήεσσι θοῇσι
νήπιος,
sentences.tr:
all’ ouch Hyrtakidēs ethel’ Asios orchamos andrōn
authi lipein hippous te kai hēniochon theraponta,
alla syn autoisin pelasen nēessi thoēisi
nēpios,
sentences.l:
But not Hyrtacus’-son, Asius, chief of men,
was willing there to leave the horses and the charioteer, his attendant,
but along with them drove close to the swift ships,
foolish,
sentences.i: But Asius, son of Hyrtacus, chief of men, was not willing to leave his horses and his attendant charioteer behind there, and instead drove up with them to the swift ships, foolish as he was,
sentences.n: Asius refuses the plan. ἔθελ’ is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘be willing’ and αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν is a stock phrase, ‘chief of men’. ἡνίοχον θεράποντα is ‘a charioteer, an attendant’: θεράπων ‘attendant’ names what the driver is to his lord. σὺν αὐτοῖσιν is ‘along with them’, the horses and the driver, and πέλασεν is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring close’; the Greek leaves out what he brought, which is the chariot and its team. νήεσσι θοῇσι is the epic dative plural, ‘to the swift ships’. νήπιος ‘foolish’ is the poet’s own comment on a man he knows to be doomed. The sentence is six lines long, so the unit stops at the comma in the middle of line 113.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε κακὰς ὑπὸ κῆρας ἀλύξας
ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν ἀγαλλόμενος παρὰ νηῶν
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ emelle kakas hypo kēras alyxas
hippoisin kai ochesphin agallomenos para nēōn
aps aponostēsein proti Ilion ēnemoessan·
sentences.i: and he was not, as it turned out, to escape the evil fates of death and go back from the ships to windy Ilios, exulting in his horses and chariot;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 113. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε is ‘and, as it turned out, he was not going to’, with the future infinitive ἀπονοστήσειν ‘return home’. κῆρας is the plural of κήρ ‘death-fate’, not κῆρ ‘heart’, and ἀλύξας is the aorist participle of ἀλύσκω ‘escape’; ὑπό with the accusative gives ‘from under’ the fates. ἀγαλλόμενος is ‘exulting’, and ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν is the dative of what he exults in, ‘horses and chariot’. παρὰ νηῶν is ‘from beside the ships’, ἂψ ‘back’, προτί the epic form of πρός, and ἠνεμόεσσαν ‘windy’ the stock epithet of Ilios. The last line is already in the poem (8.499), and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
πρόσθεν γάρ μιν μοῖρα δυσώνυμος ἀμφεκάλυψεν
ἔγχεϊ Ἰδομενῆος ἀγαυοῦ Δευκαλίδαο.
sentences.tr:
prosthen gar min moira dysōnymos amphekalypsen
encheï Idomenēos agauou Deukalidao.
sentences.l:
For before that, him a portion, ill-named, enfolded
with the spear of Idomeneus, the noble, Deucalion’s-son.
sentences.i: For before that, through the spear of noble Idomeneus, son of Deucalion, an ill-named fate had enfolded him.
sentences.n: Here the poet says in advance what will become of Asius. πρόσθεν γάρ is ‘for before that’, and μιν is ‘him’. μοῖρα is ‘portion’ in the literal line and ‘fate’ in the free one. δυσώνυμος is ‘ill-named’ (δυσ- ‘bad’ plus ὄνομα ‘name’), a name of ill omen. ἀμφεκάλυψεν is the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω ‘enfold’ (literally ‘cover round’), the picture of death closing over a man. ἔγχεϊ is the dative of means, ‘by the spear’. Ἰδομενῆος is the epic genitive of Ἰδομενεύς, ἀγαυοῦ is ‘noble’, and Δευκαλίδαο is the patronymic ‘son of Deucalion’, with the genitive ending -αο.

sentences.t:
εἴσατο γὰρ νηῶν ἐπ’ ἀριστερά, τῇ περ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐκ πεδίου νίσοντο σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφι·
sentences.tr:
eisato gar nēōn ep’ aristera, tēi per Achaioi
ek pediou nisonto syn hippoisin kai ochesphi·
sentences.l:
For he made for the left of the ships, where the Achaeans
from the plain were returning with horses and chariots;
sentences.i: For he had gone to the left of the ships, where the Achaeans were coming back from the plain with their horses and chariots;
sentences.n: γάρ explains how Asius could drive up to the wall at all. εἴσατο is read here as the aorist middle of ἵεμαι ‘rush, make for’; its stem is the same as in εἴσαντο ‘seemed’ at 103 (from εἴδομαι), but the sense ‘seemed’ does not fit here. νηῶν ἐπ’ ἀριστερά is ‘to the left of the ships’, with ἀριστερά the neuter plural used as ‘the left side’. τῇ περ is ‘just where’, and νίσοντο is the imperfect of νίσομαι ‘go, return’, ‘were coming back’. σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφι is ‘with horses and chariots’.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥ’ ἵππους τε καὶ ἅρμα διήλασεν, οὐδὲ πύλῃσιν
εὗρ’ ἐπικεκλιμένας σανίδας καὶ μακρὸν ὀχῆα,
ἀλλ’ ἀναπεπταμένας ἔχον ἀνέρες, εἴ τιν’ ἑταίρων
ἐκ πολέμου φεύγοντα σαώσειαν μετὰ νῆας.
sentences.tr:
tēi rh’ hippous te kai harma diēlasen, oude pylēisin
heur’ epikeklimenas sanidas kai makron ochēa,
all’ anapeptamenas echon aneres, ei tin’ hetairōn
ek polemou pheugonta saōseian meta nēas.
sentences.l:
that way he drove through horses and chariot, and in the gates
he found neither the doors shut to nor the long bar,
but thrown open the men were keeping them, in case any of their companions
fleeing from the war they might save, to the ships.
sentences.i: He drove his horses and chariot through there, and in the gates he found neither the doors shut to nor the long bar; the men kept them thrown open, in case they might save some companion fleeing from the war toward the ships.
sentences.n: τῇ ‘that way’ is the left-hand passage of the last unit. διήλασεν is the aorist of διελαύνω ‘drive through’. ἐπικεκλιμένας is the perfect passive participle of ἐπικλίνω ‘lean to, shut’. σανίδας is literally ‘boards’ and here the door-leaves, so ‘doors’; ὀχῆα is the accusative of ὀχεύς ‘bar’. ἀναπεπταμένας is the perfect passive participle of ἀναπετάννυμι ‘spread open’, and ἔχον is the imperfect, ‘were keeping’. ἀνέρες is the epic ἄνδρες, ‘men’, the Achaean guards. εἴ τιν’ … σαώσειαν is εἰ with the optative of purpose, ‘in case they might save’, and ἑταίρων is ‘companions’. The gate stands open for fugitives; Asius drives in by it.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥ’ ἰθὺς φρονέων ἵππους ἔχε, τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο
ὀξέα κεκλήγοντες·
sentences.tr:
tēi rh’ ithys phroneōn hippous eche, toi d’ ham’ heponto
oxea keklēgontes·
sentences.l:
That way straight, in his purpose, he held the horses, and they followed with him,
shrilly shrieking;
sentences.i: That way he held his horses straight on, intent, and his men followed along with shrill cries;
sentences.n: ἰθύς ‘straight’ and φρονέων, a participle ‘having it in mind’ with no object stated, together give ‘straight on, intent’. ἔχε is the imperfect of ἔχω, here ‘kept on course’. τοὶ δ’ is ‘and they’, the men following, and ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. ὀξέα κεκλήγοντες is ‘shrilly shrieking’: κεκλήγοντες is a perfect participle of κλάζω with present force, and ὀξέα is the neuter plural used as an adverb. The unit ends in the middle of line 125, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἔφαντο γὰρ οὐκ ἔτ’ Ἀχαιοὺς
σχήσεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἐν νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν πεσέεσθαι
νήπιοι,
sentences.tr:
ephanto gar ouk et’ Achaious
schēsesth’, all’ en nēusi melainēisin peseesthai
nēpioi,
sentences.l:
for they said that no longer the Achaeans
would hold back, but upon the black ships would fall,
foolish ones,
sentences.i: for they thought that the Achaeans would no longer hold back, but would fall upon the black ships, foolish as they were,
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 125. ἔφαντο is the imperfect middle of φημί, ‘they said’, and takes the accusative Ἀχαιούς and the infinitives σχήσεσθ’ and πεσέεσθαι. Line 126 is the same line as 107, and its English is the one it already has in iliad-054; but the subject of the infinitives is now named, ‘the Achaeans’, so the Trojans are saying that it is the Achaeans who will no longer hold out and will fall at the ships; the English of the repeated line is kept as it stands. νήπιοι ‘foolish ones’ is again the poet’s comment on men he knows to be wrong. The unit ends at the comma in the middle of line 127.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ πύλῃσι δύ’ ἀνέρας εὗρον ἀρίστους
υἷας ὑπερθύμους Λαπιθάων αἰχμητάων,
τὸν μὲν Πειριθόου υἷα κρατερὸν Πολυποίτην,
τὸν δὲ Λεοντῆα βροτολοιγῷ ἶσον Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.tr:
en de pylēisi dy’ aneras heuron aristous
huias hyperthymous Lapithaōn aichmētaōn,
ton men Peirithoou huia krateron Polypoitēn,
ton de Leontēa brotoloigōi ison Arēï.
sentences.l:
and in the gates two men they found, the best,
high-spirited sons of the Lapiths, the spearmen,
the one, Peirithous’ son, strong Polypoetes,
the other, Leonteus, equal to mortal-ruining Ares.
sentences.i: and in the gates they found two men, the best, high-spirited sons of the Lapith spearmen: one, strong Polypoetes, the son of Peirithous, and the other Leonteus, the equal of Ares, the ruin of mortals.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 127; ἐν δὲ πύλῃσι ‘and in the gates’ gives the second half of the sentence. εὗρον is ‘they found’, the subject being Asius and his men. δύ’ is δύο, ἀνέρας is ἄνδρας ‘men’, and υἷας is in apposition. ὑπερθύμους is ‘high-spirited’. Λαπιθάων αἰχμητάων has the epic genitive ending -άων, ‘of the Lapiths, the spearmen’. τὸν μὲν … τὸν δέ is ‘the one … the other’, with the article as pronoun. Πειριθόου is the genitive of Πειρίθοος, and Πολυποίτην and Λεοντῆα are accusatives. βροτολοιγός is βροτός ‘mortal’ plus λοιγός ‘ruin’, the stock epithet of Ares.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἄρα προπάροιθε πυλάων ὑψηλάων
ἕστασαν ὡς ὅτε τε δρύες οὔρεσιν ὑψικάρηνοι,
αἵ τ’ ἄνεμον μίμνουσι καὶ ὑετὸν ἤματα πάντα
ῥίζῃσιν μεγάλῃσι διηνεκέεσσ’ ἀραρυῖαι·
sentences.tr:
tō men ara proparoithe pylaōn hypsēlaōn
hestasan hōs hote te dryes ouresin hypsikarēnoi,
hai t’ anemon mimnousi kai hyeton ēmata panta
rhizēisin megalēisi diēnekeess’ araruiai·
sentences.l:
The two before the gates, the high ones,
were standing, as when oaks on the mountains, high-headed,
which the wind await and the rain all days,
with great roots, unbroken, fitted;
sentences.i: The two stood before the high gates, like high-headed oaks on the mountains, which withstand the wind and the rain every day, held fast by their great, unbroken roots;
sentences.n: τὼ … ἕστασαν ‘the two stood’ is the dual article as pronoun with ἕστασαν, a pluperfect of ἵστημι used as an imperfect, ‘were standing’. πυλάων ὑψηλάων has the epic genitive plural; ὑψηλός is ‘high’. ὡς ὅτε τε is ‘as when’, which opens the simile. δρύες is ‘oaks’, οὔρεσιν the epic dative plural ‘on the mountains’, and ὑψικάρηνοι ‘high-headed’ is ὑψι- ‘high’ plus κάρηνον ‘head, top’. αἵ τ’ is the relative ‘which’; μίμνουσι is ‘wait for, withstand’. ῥίζῃσιν μεγάλῃσι διηνεκέεσσ’ ἀραρυῖαι is ‘fitted with great, unbroken roots’: διηνεκής is ‘unbroken, continuous’, and ἀραρυῖαι is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, here ‘fixed in the ground’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τὼ χείρεσσι πεποιθότες ἠδὲ βίηφι
μίμνον ἐπερχόμενον μέγαν Ἄσιον οὐδὲ φέβοντο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara tō cheiressi pepoithotes ēde biēphi
mimnon eperchomenon megan Asion oude phebonto.
sentences.l:
So then the two, in their hands trusting and in their might,
awaited great Asius as he came on, and did not flee.
sentences.i: So the two, trusting in their hands and in their might, stood their ground against great Asius as he came on, and did not flee.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα closes the simile: ‘so then’. τὼ is the dual ‘the two’. πεποιθότες is the perfect participle of πείθω, ‘trusting’, with the dative χείρεσσι (epic dative plural) ‘in their hands’; βίηφι has the ending -φι, ‘in might’. μίμνον is the imperfect of μίμνω, ‘awaited’, the same verb as in line 133 and here with the accusative of the man coming. ἐπερχόμενον ‘advancing’ agrees with Ἄσιον, and οὐδὲ φέβοντο is ‘and did not flee’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἰθὺς πρὸς τεῖχος ἐΰδμητον βόας αὔας
ὑψόσ’ ἀνασχόμενοι ἔκιον μεγάλῳ ἀλαλητῷ
Ἄσιον ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα καὶ Ἰαμενὸν καὶ Ὀρέστην
Ἀσιάδην τ’ Ἀδάμαντα Θόωνά τε Οἰνόμαόν τε.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ithys pros teichos eÿdmēton boas auas
hypsos’ anaschomenoi ekion megalōi alalētōi
Asion amphi anakta kai Iamenon kai Orestēn
Asiadēn t’ Adamanta Thoōna te Oinomaon te.
sentences.l:
And they straight at the well-built wall, dry oxhides
held up high, went with a great outcry
around lord Asius and Iamenus and Orestes
and Adamas, Asius’-son, and Thoön and Oenomaus.
sentences.i: And they went straight at the well-built wall with a great outcry, holding their dry oxhides up high, around lord Asius and Iamenus and Orestes and Adamas, son of Asius, and Thoön and Oenomaus.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, Asius’ men, set against the two at the gate. βόας αὔας is ‘dry oxhides’, shields of hide; ἀνασχόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’, and ὑψόσ’ is ὑψόσε ‘up high’. ἐΰδμητον is ‘well-built’, the stock epithet of the wall. ἔκιον is the imperfect of κίω ‘go’, and ἀλαλητός is ‘outcry’. Ἄσιον ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα is ‘around lord Asius’, with ἄναξ ‘lord’ and ἀμφί placed between name and noun. Ἀσιάδην is the patronymic ‘son of Asius’; the other names are Iamenus, Orestes, Adamas, Thoön and Oenomaus.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἤτοι εἷος μὲν ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιοὺς
ὄρνυον ἔνδον ἐόντες ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ νηῶν·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ētoi heios men eÿknēmidas Achaious
ornyon endon eontes amynesthai peri nēōn·
sentences.l:
And they, for as long as the well-greaved Achaeans
they were urging, being within, to defend themselves about the ships;
sentences.i: As long as they were still inside, they kept urging the well-greaved Achaeans to defend themselves for the ships;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἤτοι is ‘and they’, the defenders at the gates, the two Lapiths among them; the pair are picked out again as τώ ‘those two’ in line 145. εἷος μέν is ‘for as long as’ (εἷος = ἕως) and is answered by αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ‘but when’ in the next unit. ἐϋκνήμιδας is ‘well-greaved’, from ἐΰ- ‘well’ and κνημίς ‘greave’, the stock epithet of the Achaeans. ὄρνυον is the imperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, with ἔνδον ἐόντες ‘being within’; ἀμύνεσθαι is the middle infinitive ‘defend themselves’, and περὶ νηῶν is ‘for the ships’. Ἀχαιούς is the accusative object of ὄρνυον: it is the two Lapiths who urge, and the Achaeans who are urged.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τεῖχος ἐπεσσυμένους ἐνόησαν
Τρῶας, ἀτὰρ Δαναῶν γένετο ἰαχή τε φόβος τε,
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē teichos epessymenous enoēsan
Trōas, atar Danaōn geneto iachē te phobos te,
sentences.l:
but when they perceived the Trojans rushing
on the wall, and of the Danaans came a cry and terror,
sentences.i: but when they saw the Trojans rushing at the wall, and a cry and terror rose among the Danaans,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ is ‘but when’. ἐπεσσυμένους is the perfect passive participle of ἐπισεύω ‘rush on’, in the accusative agreeing with Τρῶας, which stands at the start of the next line. ἐνόησαν is the aorist of νοέω, ‘perceived, saw’. ἀτάρ is ‘and’. The cry and the fear belong to the Danaans: Δαναῶν is the genitive ‘of the Danaans’, ἰαχή is ‘cry’ and φόβος ‘terror’ (in battle the word can also mean flight). The sentence is not finished until line 145.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ τὼ ἀΐξαντε πυλάων πρόσθε μαχέσθην
ἀγροτέροισι σύεσσιν ἐοικότε, τώ τ’ ἐν ὄρεσσιν
ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ κυνῶν δέχαται κολοσυρτὸν ἰόντα,
sentences.tr:
ek de tō aïxante pylaōn prosthe machesthēn
agroteroisi syessin eoikote, tō t’ en oressin
andrōn ēde kynōn dechatai kolosyrton ionta,
sentences.l:
out then the two, darting from the gates, fought in front,
like wild swine, which in the mountains
await an uproar of men and of dogs coming on,
sentences.i: the two darted out from the gates and fought out in front, like wild boars which in the mountains wait for the uproar of men and of dogs coming on,
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἀΐξαντε is tmesis, ‘darting out’, the aorist dual participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, and τὼ is the dual article as pronoun, ‘the two’, the Lapiths. μαχέσθην is the dual of μάχομαι, ‘the two fought’. ἀγροτέροισι σύεσσιν ἐοικότε is ‘like wild swine’, with ἐοικότε a dual participle. τώ τ’ is the relative ‘which’, in the dual like the pair of fighters; δέχαται is the epic third plural of δέχομαι, ‘wait for, receive’. κολοσυρτός is ‘a noisy crowd, an uproar’; ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ κυνῶν is ‘of men and of dogs’, and ἰόντα ‘coming on’.

sentences.t:
δοχμώ τ’ ἀΐσσοντε περὶ σφίσιν ἄγνυτον ὕλην
πρυμνὴν ἐκτάμνοντες, ὑπαὶ δέ τε κόμπος ὀδόντων
γίγνεται εἰς ὅ κέ τίς τε βαλὼν ἐκ θυμὸν ἕληται·
sentences.tr:
dochmō t’ aïssonte peri sphisin agnyton hylēn
prymnēn ektamnontes, hypai de te kompos odontōn
gignetai eis ho ke tis te balōn ek thymon helētai·
sentences.i: they dart slantwise and break the forest about them, cutting it off at the root, and a din of teeth rises from beneath, until a man strikes one and takes its life;
sentences.n: The simile of the two boars goes on in the dual: δοχμώ ‘slantwise’, ἀΐσσοντε ‘darting’ and ἄγνυτον ‘break’ (the dual imperfect of ἄγνυμι) all refer to the pair. περὶ σφίσιν is ‘about themselves’, and πρυμνὴν ‘at the root, at the base’ describes ὕλην ‘forest, timber’. ὑπαί is ὑπό ‘beneath’. κόμπος ὀδόντων is ‘a din of teeth’, the sound of the boars gnashing their tusks. εἰς ὅ κέ … ἕληται is ‘until … takes’, the aorist subjunctive ἕληται of αἱρέω with ἐκ in tmesis, and θυμός here is the ‘life’ that leaves the body. The present γίγνεται makes the picture one of what always happens in such a hunt.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν κόμπει χαλκὸς ἐπὶ στήθεσσι φαεινὸς
ἄντην βαλλομένων·
sentences.tr:
hōs tōn kompei chalkos epi stēthessi phaeinos
antēn ballomenōn·
sentences.l:
So of them clanged the bronze, shining, upon their chests,
as they were struck from in front;
sentences.i: So the shining bronze clanged on their chests as they were struck from the front;
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile and τῶν ‘of them’ is the two Lapiths again, with βαλλομένων ‘being struck’. κόμπει is the verb of κόμπος ‘din’ in the last unit: ‘clangs, rings’. χαλκὸς φαεινός is ‘shining bronze’, the bronze of their armour. ἐπὶ στήθεσσι is the epic dative plural, ‘on their chests’, and ἄντην is ‘in front, face to face’. The unit ends in the middle of line 152, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
μάλα γὰρ κρατερῶς ἐμάχοντο
λαοῖσιν καθύπερθε πεποιθότες ἠδὲ βίηφιν.
sentences.tr:
mala gar kraterōs emachonto
laoisin kathyperthe pepoithotes ēde biēphin.
sentences.l:
for very strongly they fought,
trusting in the men above and in their might.
sentences.i: for they fought very strongly, trusting in the men above them and in their might.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 152. γάρ gives the reason for the clanging: the two fought hard. κρατερῶς is ‘strongly’, and λαοῖσιν καθύπερθε is ‘the men above’, the defenders on the wall and towers, on whom the two Lapiths rely; πεποιθότες takes the dative. βίηφιν has the ending -φιν, ‘in might’, as βίηφι in line 135.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρα χερμαδίοισιν ἐϋδμήτων ἀπὸ πύργων
βάλλον ἀμυνόμενοι σφῶν τ’ αὐτῶν καὶ κλισιάων
νηῶν τ’ ὠκυπόρων·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ara chermadioisin eÿdmētōn apo pyrgōn
ballon amynomenoi sphōn t’ autōn kai klisiaōn
nēōn t’ ōkyporōn·
sentences.i: And the men on the wall threw stones from the well-built towers, defending themselves and their huts and the swift-faring ships;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they’, the men on the walls and towers. χερμαδίοισιν is the epic dative plural of χερμάδιον ‘stone’, a stone that fills the hand. ἐϋδμήτων is ‘well-built’, the same epithet as in line 137, here of the towers. ἀμυνόμενοι ‘defending’ governs the genitives that follow: σφῶν … αὐτῶν ‘themselves’, κλισιάων ‘huts’ (the epic genitive plural), and νηῶν ὠκυπόρων ‘swift-faring ships’. The unit ends in the middle of line 156, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
νιφάδες δ’ ὡς πῖπτον ἔραζε,
ἅς τ’ ἄνεμος ζαὴς νέφεα σκιόεντα δονήσας
ταρφειὰς κατέχευεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ·
sentences.tr:
niphades d’ hōs pipton eraze,
has t’ anemos zaēs nephea skioenta donēsas
tarpheias katecheuen epi chthoni poulyboteirēi·
sentences.i: and they fell to the ground like snowflakes, thick flakes which a hard-blowing wind pours down on the earth that feeds so many, after shaking the shadowy clouds;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 156. The subject of πῖπτον is the stones, not repeated; νιφάδες δ’ ὡς is ‘like snowflakes’, with ὡς placed after its noun. ἔραζε is ‘to the ground’. ἅς τ’ is the relative ‘which’, referring to the snowflakes. ἄνεμος ζαής is ‘a hard-blowing wind’ (ζα- strengthens ἄημι ‘blow’), and νέφεα σκιόεντα is ‘shadowy clouds’. δονήσας is the aorist participle of δονέω ‘shake’. ταρφειάς is ‘thick’, agreeing with ‘flakes’. κατέχευεν is a gnomic aorist, ‘poured down’ of what always happens, and the free English puts it in the present. πουλυβοτείρῃ is ‘much-nourishing’, the stock epithet of the earth.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν ἐκ χειρῶν βέλεα ῥέον ἠμὲν Ἀχαιῶν
ἠδὲ καὶ ἐκ Τρώων·
sentences.tr:
hōs tōn ek cheirōn belea rheon ēmen Achaiōn
ēde kai ek Trōōn·
sentences.l:
So of them from their hands missiles flowed, both of the Achaeans
and from the Trojans;
sentences.i: So missiles streamed from their hands, both from the Achaeans and from the Trojans;
sentences.n: Here the Greek turns the snow simile back onto the fight: ὣς τῶν ἐκ χειρῶν is ‘so from their hands’. ῥέον is the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’. ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καὶ is ‘both … and’, and the genitives Ἀχαιῶν and Τρώων name the two sides. βέλεα is the plural of βέλος, which the Iliad usually renders ‘shaft’; here it is ‘missiles’, because stones and every kind of thrown weapon are meant. The unit ends in the middle of line 160, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κόρυθες δ’ ἀμφ’ αὖον ἀΰτευν
βαλλομένων μυλάκεσσι καὶ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι.
sentences.tr:
korythes d’ amph’ auon aÿteun
ballomenōn mylakessi kai aspides omphaloessai.
sentences.l:
and helmets about rang dry
when they were struck with millstones, and the bossed shields.
sentences.i: and the helmets rang harshly all about as the men were struck with great round stones, and the bossed shields too.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 160. κόρυθες ‘helmets’ and ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι ‘bossed shields’ (ὀμφαλός ‘boss, navel’) are the subjects of ἀΰτευν, the imperfect of ἀϋτέω ‘cry out, ring’. αὖον is the neuter of αὖος ‘dry’ used as an adverb: ‘with a dry, harsh sound’. βαλλομένων is a genitive plural, ‘as they were being struck’, without a noun, the men under the helmets. μυλάκεσσι is the epic dative plural of μύλαξ, a stone as big as a millstone.

sentences.t:
δή ῥα τότ’ ᾤμωξεν καὶ ὣ πεπλήγετο μηρὼ
Ἄσιος Ὑρτακίδης, καὶ ἀλαστήσας ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
dē rha tot’ ōimōxen kai hō peplēgeto mērō
Asios Hyrtakidēs, kai alastēsas epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
Then indeed he wailed and struck his own two thighs,
Asius, Hyrtacus’-son, and, in bitter indignation, spoke a word:
sentences.i: Then Asius, son of Hyrtacus, cried out and struck both his thighs, and said in bitter indignation:
sentences.n: Asius reacts to the hail of missiles. δή ῥα τότ’ is ‘then indeed’. ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω, a cry of grief, ‘wailed, cried out’. ὣ … μηρώ is ‘his own two thighs’, with ὥ the dual of the possessive ὅς; striking the thighs is a gesture of dismay. πεπλήγετο is a reduplicated aorist middle of πλήσσω ‘strike’. ἀλαστήσας is the aorist participle of ἀλαστέω, from the root of ἄλαστος ‘not to be forgotten’; the sense is ‘be bitterly indignant’, and the exact force is not certain. ἔπος ηὔδα is ‘spoke a word’, the formula that introduces a speech.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἦ ῥά νυ καὶ σὺ φιλοψευδὴς ἐτέτυξο
πάγχυ μάλ’·
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater ē rha ny kai sy philopseudēs etetyxo
panchy mal’·
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, truly, then, you too were lie-loving
utterly, very much;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, so you too, it seems, have turned out to be fond of lies, altogether;
sentences.n: Asius begins his complaint at once, and it is aimed at Zeus. Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’. ἦ ῥά νυ is ‘truly, then’ (the weak νυ ‘now’ is not given its own word), the tone of a man who has just seen his mistake; καὶ σύ ‘you too’ is not explained, and the next line says what he had believed. φιλοψευδής is ‘lie-loving’ (φιλο- ‘fond of’ plus ψεῦδος ‘lie’). ἐτέτυξο is the second person singular of the pluperfect passive of τεύχω, ‘you were made, you turned out to be’, a pluperfect used like a simple past. πάγχυ μάλ’ is ‘utterly, very much’. This unit ends in the middle of line 165, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγ’ ἐφάμην ἥρωας Ἀχαιοὺς
σχήσειν ἡμέτερόν γε μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἀάπτους.
sentences.tr:
ou gar egōg’ ephamēn hērōas Achaious
schēsein hēmeteron ge menos kai cheiras aaptous.
sentences.l:
for I, at least, did not say that the hero Achaeans
would hold off our might and our hands, untouchable.
sentences.i: for I never thought that the Achaean heroes would hold off our might and our irresistible hands.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 165. οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγ’ is ‘for I, at least, … not’. ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί, ‘I said’, with an accusative and a future infinitive; as at 8.498–499 the free English has ‘thought’. σχήσειν is the future infinitive of ἔχω, here with an object, ‘hold off’. ἡμέτερον μένος is ‘our might’. ἀάπτους is of unknown meaning; the traditional guesses are ‘untouchable’ and ‘irresistible’, the first used in the literal line and the second in the free one.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’, ὥς τε σφῆκες μέσον αἰόλοι ἠὲ μέλισσαι
οἰκία ποιήσωνται ὁδῷ ἔπι παιπαλοέσσῃ,
οὐδ’ ἀπολείπουσιν κοῖλον δόμον, ἀλλὰ μένοντες
ἄνδρας θηρητῆρας ἀμύνονται περὶ τέκνων,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’, hōs te sphēkes meson aioloi ēe melissai
oikia poiēsōntai hodōi epi paipaloessēi,
oud’ apoleipousin koilon domon, alla menontes
andras thērētēras amynontai peri teknōn,
sentences.l:
but they, as wasps, in the middle quick-moving, or bees,
when they have made their homes by a rugged road,
and do not leave their hollow house, but staying
ward off the hunters, men, for their children,
sentences.i: But they are like wasps, nimble at the waist, or bees, which make their homes by a rugged road and do not leave their hollow house, but stay and ward off the hunters for the sake of their young,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘but they’, the Achaeans; the comparison with wasps and bees is completed by ὣς οἵ γε in the next unit. ὥς τε is ‘like, as’, and the general statement is put in the subjunctive: ποιήσωνται, ‘when they have made’. σφῆκες μέσον αἰόλοι is ‘wasps quick-moving in the middle’: αἰόλος is ‘quick-moving, darting’ (also ‘flashing’), and μέσον is probably ‘in the middle’, the waist, but the sense is not settled; the free English takes ‘nimble at the waist’. ὁδῷ ἔπι παιπαλοέσσῃ is ‘by a rugged road’, with ἔπι after its noun; παιπαλόεις is ‘rugged’. κοῖλον δόμον is ‘a hollow house’. ἀμύνονται is ‘ward off’, here with the object ἄνδρας θηρητῆρας ‘hunters’, and περὶ τέκνων is ‘for the sake of their children’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἵ γ’ οὐκ ἐθέλουσι πυλάων καὶ δύ’ ἐόντε
χάσσασθαι πρίν γ’ ἠὲ κατακτάμεν ἠὲ ἁλῶναι.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi g’ ouk ethelousi pylaōn kai dy’ eonte
chassasthai prin g’ ēe kataktamen ēe halōnai.
sentences.l:
so these, too, are not willing, from the gates, though being only two,
to give way, before killing or being taken.”
sentences.i: so these two are unwilling to give way from the gates, even though they are only two, before they have killed or been taken.”
sentences.n: ὣς οἵ γ’ completes the comparison: ‘so these’, the Lapiths at the gate. ἐθέλουσι is ‘are willing’, and χάσσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of χάζομαι ‘give way’, with the genitive πυλάων ‘from the gates’. καὶ δύ’ ἐόντε is ‘even though being only two’, with ἐόντε a dual participle. πρίν γ’ ἠὲ … ἠὲ is ‘before either … or’. κατακτάμεν is an epic infinitive, ‘to kill’, with no object named, and ἁλῶναι is the aorist infinitive of ἁλίσκομαι (passive in sense) ‘be taken’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδὲ Διὸς πεῖθε φρένα ταῦτ’ ἀγορεύων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oude Dios peithe phrena taut’ agoreuōn·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and not the mind of Zeus did he persuade, saying these things;
sentences.i: So he spoke, but in saying these things he did not persuade the mind of Zeus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech. οὐδὲ … πεῖθε is the imperfect of πείθω, ‘did not persuade’, with φρένα ‘mind’ as its object, and ταῦτ’ ἀγορεύων is ‘saying these things’. The next unit gives Zeus’ reason.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορι γάρ οἱ θυμὸς ἐβούλετο κῦδος ὀρέξαι.
sentences.tr: Hektori gar hoi thymos ebouleto kydos orexai.
sentences.l: for to Hector his heart was wishing to grant glory.
sentences.i: for his heart wished to grant glory to Hector.
sentences.n: γάρ gives Zeus’ reason for ignoring Asius. οἱ is ‘his’ (Zeus’), and θυμός is ‘heart’. ἐβούλετο is the imperfect of βούλομαι ‘wish’, ὀρέξαι the aorist infinitive of ὀρέγω ‘reach out, grant’, and κῦδος is ‘glory’.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι δ’ ἀμφ’ ἄλλῃσι μάχην ἐμάχοντο πύλῃσιν·
sentences.tr: alloi d’ amph’ allēisi machēn emachonto pylēisin·
sentences.l: And others about other gates fought the fight;
sentences.i: And others were fighting the battle about other gates;
sentences.n: The poet turns from this gate to the others. ἄλλοι … ἄλλῃσι ‘others … at other’ repeats the word to show the fighting spread everywhere. μάχην ἐμάχοντο is ‘fought a fight’, a verb with its own noun as object, and πύλῃσιν is the epic dative plural ‘gates’.

sentences.t: ἀργαλέον δέ με ταῦτα θεὸν ὣς πάντ’ ἀγορεῦσαι·
sentences.tr: argaleon de me tauta theon hōs pant’ agoreusai·
sentences.l: but hard it is for me, as a god, all these things to tell;
sentences.i: but it is hard for me to tell all this, as if I were a god;
sentences.n: The poet speaks in his own person. ἀργαλέον is ‘hard’, and με ἀγορεῦσαι is the accusative and infinitive ‘for me to tell’, the aorist infinitive of ἀγορεύω. θεὸν ὥς is ‘like a god’, with ὥς placed after its noun: a god could see and tell the whole battle, a man cannot. ταῦτα πάντ’ is ‘all these things’.

sentences.t:
πάντῃ γὰρ περὶ τεῖχος ὀρώρει θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ
λάϊνον·
sentences.tr:
pantēi gar peri teichos orōrei thespidaes pyr
laïnon·
sentences.l:
for everywhere about the wall had risen wondrous-blazing fire,
of stone;
sentences.i: for on every side around the wall a wondrous-blazing fire of stone had risen;
sentences.n: πάντῃ is ‘on every side’. ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘had risen’. θεσπιδαές is ‘wondrous-blazing’ (θέσπις ‘wondrous’ plus δαίω ‘burn’), the Odyssey’s rendering. λάϊνον is ‘of stone’, which makes the phrase ‘a fire of stone’; the usual understanding is that this is the poet’s picture of the hail of stones. The unit ends in the middle of line 178, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δὲ καὶ ἀχνύμενοί περ ἀνάγκῃ
νηῶν ἠμύνοντο·
sentences.tr:
Argeioi de kai achnymenoi per anankēi
nēōn ēmynonto·
sentences.l:
and the Argives, even though grieving, by necessity
were defending the ships;
sentences.i: and the Argives, though grieving, were defending the ships of necessity;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 178. ἀχνύμενοί περ is ‘even though grieving’, περ marking the concession. ἀνάγκῃ is ‘by necessity’, the dative of cause. ἠμύνοντο is the imperfect of ἀμύνομαι ‘defend’, here with the genitive νηῶν ‘the ships’. The unit ends in the middle of line 179, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
θεοὶ δ’ ἀκαχήατο θυμὸν
πάντες ὅσοι Δαναοῖσι μάχης ἐπιτάρροθοι ἦσαν.
sentences.tr:
theoi d’ akachēato thymon
pantes hosoi Danaoisi machēs epitarrothoi ēsan.
sentences.l:
and the gods were grieved in heart,
all who to the Danaans in battle were helpers.
sentences.i: and all the gods who were helpers to the Danaans in battle were grieved at heart.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 179. ἀκαχήατο is the pluperfect passive of ἀκαχίζω ‘grieve’, the verb of ἀκαχήμενος ‘grieved’, here ‘were grieved’; θυμόν is the accusative of respect, ‘in heart’. πάντες ὅσοι is ‘all who’, and Δαναοῖσι is the dative ‘to the Danaans’. ἐπιτάρροθοι is ‘helpers’, a rare word of unclear formation, so the note gives its sense only; μάχης is the genitive ‘in battle’.

sentences.t: σὺν δ’ ἔβαλον Λαπίθαι πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα.
sentences.tr: syn d’ ebalon Lapithai polemon kai dēïotēta.
sentences.l: And together they threw, the Lapiths, war and fighting.
sentences.i: And the Lapiths joined war and fighting together.
sentences.n: σὺν δ’ ἔβαλον is tmesis for συμβάλλω ‘throw together’, and with πόλεμον the phrase is the idiom for joining battle. Λαπίθαι is ‘the Lapiths’, the people of Polypoetes and Leonteus. πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα is ‘war and fighting’, two nouns for the same thing; δηϊοτής is ‘fighting, slaughter’, from δήϊος ‘hostile’.
